title: What He Left Behind
year: 11 AH — 632 CE, and every year after it
teaser: He owned nothing at the end. What he left instead has outlasted every empire that existed in his lifetime.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: Seven dinars, and an armour in pawn
layers.content:
Count the estate first, because it is short. He died owing thirty measures of barley on a coat of armour left in pledge with a Jew of Madinah. On the Sunday before, he had freed his slaves, given away the seven dinars he owned, and handed his weapons to the Muslims. No palace, no treasury, nothing to divide.

Now count what was standing.

al-Mubarakpuri's summing-up is worth reading slowly. The call had prevailed over the whole of Arabia. Men who had carved idols were breaking them with their own hands. The adhan was going out five times a day across country that had been silent, and reciters and memorisers of the Qur'an were travelling north and south with the text in their heads. Tribes that had raided each other for generations were one people. There were no longer masters and slaves in the old sense, no men bound to other men, no aggressors holding a licence to aggress.

He had put it in one sentence in the sermon at Arafat, and it is the shortest description of what he had done to that society: an Arab is no better than a non-Arab, and a non-Arab no better than an Arab; a red man is no better than a black one except in piety; humanity is all of Adam's children, and Adam was created from dust.

The scale is measurable across a single decade. Ten thousand men marched on Makkah in the eighth year. Thirty thousand marched to Tabuk in the ninth. In the tenth, the crowd at the Farewell Pilgrimage is put somewhere between a hundred thousand and a hundred and forty-four thousand — the reports differ — and al-Mubarakpuri describes it as an ocean of men whose voices shook the ground.

None of that is the inheritance. It is the evidence that there was one. What follows is the accounting: the man, the Book, the community, and what reaches a reader who was never in the room.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Man
layers.subtitle: Twenty grey hairs and a bundle of firewood
layers.content:
Begin with what he looked like, because the sources bothered to record it. Umm Ma'bad, who saw him once as he passed her tent, told her husband he had a broad face, black eyes under finely arched brows, glossy black hair inclined to curl, a commanding voice, and an expression that was reflective. Then she said the thing everyone who met him ends up saying: a stranger would be fascinated from a distance, but the closer he came the more respect he found. Al-Bara' was asked whether his face was radiant like a sword. No, he said — like the moon. Anas reported that at his death there were about twenty grey hairs in his head and beard together.

Aishah gave the working rule of his conduct. Given a choice between two courses he took the easier and more convenient one, unless it involved sin, and then he was further from it than anybody. He never took revenge for himself. When the sanctity of Allah was violated he avenged it, and that was for Allah's sake and not his own.

He was the last to become angry and the first to be satisfied. Jabir said he never refused anything he was asked for. Ibn Abbas said he gave more freely than the blowing wind. Ali said that when a fight grew fierce and men's eyes went red they fell back on the Prophet ﷺ, because he was always the one closest to the enemy. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said he was shier than a virgin.

He repaired his own shoes and mended his own clothes. He milked the sheep. He sat at the end of a gathering next to the last man, and told others to do the same. He never blamed a servant for something left undone.

Once on a journey food had to be prepared, and his Companions divided the work — I will slaughter, I will skin it, I will cook. He said: I will collect the firewood. They told him no, they would do that as well. He said: I know that you can do it for me, but I hate to be privileged, and Allah hates to see a servant of His privileged over others. Then he went and collected the firewood.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the descriptions of his appearance and manners, and Aishah on his choices; Umm Ma'bad's description as preserved in Zad al-Ma'ad
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Book
layers.subtitle: Reviewed twice, then left in their hands
layers.content:
Of everything he handed over, one item was not his to alter, and it is the only thing he named as a bequest.

In the sermon at Arafat he said: verily, I have left among you the Book of Allah — if you hold fast to it, you shall never go astray. He did not say he was leaving them a state, or a dynasty, or a set of offices. He named a text.

That text was closed before he was. «الْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ» — 'This day I have perfected your religion for you.' (5:3) came down in that same valley within minutes of the sermon, and Umar wept, because he understood what a finished thing implies about the man who finished it. Nothing was left half-revealed for a successor to complete.

Two details of that final year bear on its preservation. In Ramadan of the tenth year he withdrew into the mosque for twenty days rather than the usual ten, and in that year the angel Jibreel went through the Qur'an with him twice instead of once. Whatever else that review was, it was a checking of the text against its source, carried out at the end.

And it was not held in one place. al-Mubarakpuri describes reciters and memorisers of the Qur'an setting out northwards and southwards across the peninsula, carrying the verses and their injunctions with them. The Book was distributed into human memory across a thousand miles of desert before the man who received it died.

The guarantee attached to it is inside it. «إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحَافِظُونَ» — 'Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian.' (15:9)

This is the hinge of the whole inheritance. A character cannot be handed on directly; it can only be described, and descriptions decay. A community cannot be handed on; it changes with every generation that holds it. A fixed text can be handed on exactly. Everything else a reader receives, they receive through it.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim — 'I have left among you the Book of Allah', from the sermon at Arafat
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: Four verses fixing what he is and is not
layers.content:
Four verses do most of the work of settling what he was, and each closes off a different way of getting him wrong.

The first makes him the standard. «لَقَدْ كَانَ لَكُمْ فِي رَسُولِ اللَّهِ أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ» — 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern.' (33:21) The measure of conduct is not a list of principles but a documented human life, which is why the sources took the trouble to record how he sat in a gathering, how he spoke to a servant, and what he did when there was firewood to fetch.

The second states the reach. «وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ إِلَّا رَحْمَةً لِلْعَالَمِينَ» — 'And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.' (21:107) Not to one tribe, and not to one century.

The third is the verdict on the character itself, and al-Mubarakpuri closes his account of the man's manners by quoting it. «وَإِنَّكَ لَعَلَىٰ خُلُقٍ عَظِيمٍ» — 'And indeed, you are of a great moral character.' (68:4) He was, al-Mubarakpuri writes, brought up and educated and taught by Allah. The praise is not his followers' opinion of him.

The fourth sets the limit, and it is the one Abu Bakr had to say out loud to a collapsing crowd. «وَمَا مُحَمَّدٌ إِلَّا رَسُولٌ» — 'Muhammad is no more than a Messenger.' (3:144) The same Book that makes him the pattern for everybody forbids anybody to worship him. Days before he died he had said it himself from the pulpit: do not make my grave a worshipped idol.

Together they settle the odd position he occupies. He is to be imitated in detail and not venerated as divine, and both halves are required. Drop the first and the religion turns into an abstraction with no shape. Drop the second and it stops being his religion at all.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, and Muatta' Imam Malik — 'Do not make my grave a worshipped idol'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What He Left Behind
layers.subtitle: A community, and a reader who was not there
layers.content:
The community was the third thing, and it was built to run without him.

He had trained men by example rather than instruction, and al-Mubarakpuri notes what became of them: the commanders he taught went on to outmatch the Persians and the Byzantines in strategy and leadership. The army he mobilised under Usamah bin Zaid in his last weeks marched out under Abu Bakr instead. Nothing had to be invented for it to move.

He had also fixed the community's shape from the valley at Arafat, in a list short enough to hold in one hand: pray the five prayers, fast Ramadan, pay the zakat of your provision willingly, make the pilgrimage to the Sacred House, and obey those in charge of you. That was the whole standing order. It still is.

His own household was small. He married thirteen women, and nine survived him. Of his four daughters, Fatimah followed him within six months, exactly as he had whispered to her on his last day. No son of his reached adulthood. There was no dynasty for anything to descend through.

Which leaves the reader.

The last thing he said from the grey mule at Mina, closing the final sermon of his life, was about people who were not present: let him that is present convey it to him who is absent, for to whom the message is conveyed may have more understanding of it than the audience. He told a crowd that had walked for days to reach him that it might land deeper in someone they would never meet.

Carry this. Thirty-one chapters have described a man — an orphan, a shepherd, a trader they called al-Amin, a husband who mourned one wife for the rest of his life, a refugee, a bricklayer on his own mosque, a commander who lost at Uhud, a man who pardoned the city that had tortured him, and at the end a patient with a fever, freeing his slaves and settling a debt of three dirhams. The point was never that he was extraordinary. It was that he is imitable. The verse calls him an excellent pattern, and a pattern is only useful to somebody holding cloth.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the sermon on the Day of Slaughter, and Sahih Muslim for the standing order given at Arafat
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: In the sermon at Arafat, what did the Prophet ﷺ name as the thing he was leaving among them?

options.text: The mosque at Madinah and its endowments
The Book of Allah — hold fast to it and you shall never go astray
The Charter of Islamic Alliance
His household, as guardians of the religion

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, quoted in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the sermon at Arafat
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was standing in front of well over a hundred thousand people who would have accepted any institution he named. He named a text.

quiz.prompt: What changed about the Prophet's Ramadan and his review of the Qur'an in the tenth year of the Hijra?

options.text: He stopped fasting because of illness
He secluded himself in the mosque for twenty days instead of ten, and Jibreel reviewed the Qur'an with him twice instead of once
He dictated the entire Qur'an to Zayd bin Thabit in one sitting
He performed Ramadan in Makkah rather than Madinah

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Symptoms of Farewell
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar lists both as signs that the end was near. They are also the two things you would do if you were closing an account: double the retreat, and check the text twice against its source.

quiz.prompt: About how much grey hair did he have at the time of his death?

options.text: None at all
His head and beard had gone entirely white
Around twenty grey hairs in head and beard together, with some at his temples
He dyed it, so it is not recorded

quiz.citation: Anas bin Malik, in Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — His Physical Appearance
quiz.scholar_reflection: Someone counted. That is the level of detail the Companions preserved about him, and it is why the phrase 'an excellent pattern' has anything concrete to attach to.

quiz.prompt: On a journey, his Companions divided up the work of preparing food between them. What did he do?

options.text: He rested while they worked, as was his right as their leader
He supervised and corrected the distribution of tasks
He said he would collect the firewood, and did it despite their objections
He ordered them to give the meat away to travellers instead

quiz.citation: Ash-Shifa', cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Perfection of Soul and Nobility
quiz.scholar_reflection: His reason is the striking part. He did not say he wanted to help. He said: I know you can do it for me, but I hate to be privileged, and Allah hates to see a servant of His privileged over others.

quiz.prompt: Which verse does al-Mubarakpuri use to close his account of the Prophet's character and manners?

options.text: 'Muhammad is no more than a Messenger' (3:144)
'And indeed, you are of a great moral character' (68:4)
'Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder' (15:9)
'This day I have perfected your religion for you' (5:3)

quiz.citation: Quran 68:4 — al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, closing The Prophet's Character and Manners
quiz.scholar_reflection: He adds a line worth keeping: the Prophet ﷺ was brought up, educated and taught by Allah. On that reading the character is not an achievement to be admired but a curriculum to be followed.

quiz.prompt: Umm Ma'bad said a stranger would be fascinated by him from a distance, but the closer he came the more respect he found. Most reputations work the other way. What do you take from that?

options.text: There was nothing being managed — the private man matched the public one
It is the single hardest test any leader can be put to
It says as much about how carefully the Companions watched him
It makes me uneasy about how I would fare under that inspection

quiz.slider_label: Admired at a distance — Trusted up close
quiz.citation: Umm Ma'bad's description, preserved in Zad al-Ma'ad and cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: She had met him once, briefly, on a road. She was not a follower at the time. It is the testimony of someone with no reason to flatter him.

quiz.prompt: He governed the whole of Arabia and died with an armour in pawn for barley and a household that had to borrow lamp oil. How do you read that?

options.text: It is the proof that the whole thing was never about gain
It is a standard for leadership that almost nobody has met since
He gave it all away in his last days; it was a choice, not a condition
It is admirable and I would not choose it, which is worth admitting

quiz.slider_label: A condition he accepted — A choice he made
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — A Day Before His Death
quiz.scholar_reflection: Both readings have support. He lived simply for years, and he also deliberately emptied his hands in the last days — freeing his slaves, giving away seven dinars, handing over his weapons.

quiz.prompt: One verse makes his life the pattern to copy; another forbids treating him as anything more than a Messenger. Which of the two is harder to hold onto?

options.text: The first — copying a person is far more demanding than admiring one
The second — love tends to inflate its object without noticing
Neither is hard in principle; both are hard in practice
They hold each other up, and drop one and the other goes too

quiz.slider_label: Hard to imitate — Hard not to venerate
quiz.scholar_reflection: He anticipated the second problem himself and named it from the pulpit five days before he died: do not make my grave a worshipped idol. That is a man auditing his own funeral.

quiz.prompt: No son of his survived, his daughter Fatimah followed him within six months, and he left no written appointment. What does an inheritance with no heir mean?

options.text: That the religion was never anybody's property to pass down
That it forced the community to decide, which had costs
That the Book was the heir, and everyone holds it equally
That the loss was real and the arrangement still worked

quiz.slider_label: A gap he left — A door he closed
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Prophetic Household
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar records the succession being argued out at Bani Sa'idah while his body still lay on the bed. The argument happened because there was nothing to inherit in the ordinary sense.

quiz.prompt: Thirty-two chapters, from an orphan in Makkah to a grave under a bed in Madinah. What is a reader meant to do with the account?

options.text: Copy one specific thing from it, starting this week
Know the man, so that the religion has a face and not just rules
Pass it on — that was the last instruction he gave about it
Sit with it honestly before deciding what it asks of me

quiz.slider_label: Learn about him — Live like him
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — 'Let him that is present convey it to him who is absent', from the sermon on the Day of Slaughter
quiz.scholar_reflection: He ended his last full sermon by talking about people who were not in the valley. If you have read this far, you are one of the people he was describing.
